result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.node_redundancy()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the redundancy coefficient of nodes in a bipartite graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L12001-L12084){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.node_redundancy(nodes=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Node redundancy](/assets/graphs/node-redundancy.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same people and events graph. ann attended party and talk, and bob attended both too, so the pair stays linked without ann: ann scores 1.0, and bob, covered by ann, also 1.0. cy is the only one at both talk and game, so the edges joining them, in the accent color, are the pair's sole link and cy scores 0.0." width="100%"} The redundancy of a node (Latapy et al., 2008) is the fraction of pairs of its neighbors that are also linked through some other node: if a person attends two events, would the two events still share an attendee without that person? A redundancy of 1 means the node's co-memberships are all duplicated by others, so removing it would not change the projection onto the other side; a redundancy of 0 means the node is the only link between each pair of its groups (a broker). Every node reported must have at least two neighbors. Edge direction and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional nodes (IDs or labels) to report. If `None` (default), all nodes. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node ID to its redundancy, between 0 and 1. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a reported node has fewer than two neighbors, or a node does not exist. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For a node with $n$ neighbors, every one of the $n(n - 1)/2$ neighbor pairs is checked for a common neighbor other than the node. Matches NetworkX's `bipartite.node_redundancy`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Ann's two events are also shared by Bob, so Ann is fully redundant; Cy is the only person linking the talk and the game: ::: {#f5869d1e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["ann", "bob", "cy", "party", "talk", "game"]) g.add_edges( [("ann", "party"), ("ann", "talk"), ("bob", "party"), ("bob", "talk"), ("cy", "talk"), ("cy", "game")] ) red = g.node_redundancy(nodes=["ann", "bob", "cy"]) {g.get_label_from_id(n): r for n, r in red.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'ann': 1.0, 'bob': 1.0, 'cy': 0.0} ``` ::: :::
